citation: Richardson, Jennifer C., & Swan, Karen. (2003). Examining social presence in online courses in relation to students' perceived learning and satisfaction. Journal of Asynchronous Learning Networks, 7(1), 68-88.
discipline: educational technology / distance & online learning (social presence theory, CMC tradition)
thesis: Reroutes the standard complaint against online learning (lack of physical co-presence) toward social presence as the actually relevant variable, and tests empirically, on n=97 completers of Empire State College's fully asynchronous SLN online courses (spring 2000), whether students' perceived social presence relates to and predicts their perceived learning and their satisfaction with the instructor; finds both relations significant, social presence a significant regression predictor of perceived learning (R2=.46), and gender (but not age or credits earned) a small but significant correlate of perceived social presence.

sections.title: I. Introduction
sections.summary: Frames online learning's promoted advantages (flexibility, anonymity, asynchronicity) against critics' complaint that it lacks face-to-face interaction, then reroutes the debate: the relevant variable is not physical co-location but social presence and teacher immediacy. Reviews social-presence theory's origin (Short, Williams & Christie's medium-salience definition), the Gunawardena & Zittle 'culturing' revision (social presence as partly a property of communicators, not only the medium), and the teacher-immediacy literature (Wiener & Mehrabian) as a related, possibly subsumed, construct.

sections.title: II. Methodology
sections.summary: Purpose: examine social presence's relation to perceived learning and instructor satisfaction in online courses. Four hypotheses (overall relation; social presence as predictor of learning; gender/age/credits as correlates of social presence; per-activity social presence vs. per-activity perceived learning). Subjects: n=97 respondents (of 369 enrolled) from ESC's SUNY Learning Network online courses, spring 2000; mostly returning/nontraditional students, 63% female. Instrument: a social-presence scale adapted from Gunawardena & Zittle, with demographic items, 16 overall Likert items (social presence, perceived learning, instructor satisfaction), and per-activity indicator items across six course-activity types, plus two open-ended questions. Correlational design (not causal); direct-entry regression for the predictor hypothesis.

sections.title: III. Analyses
sections.summary: Overall scores: social presence correlates .68 with perceived learning and .60 with instructor satisfaction; instructor satisfaction correlates .73 with perceived learning (all p<.05). Regression: social presence significantly predicts perceived learning (R2=.46). Gender correlates .219 with social presence (women higher; R2=.047); age and credits earned do not. Per-activity: social presence-learning correlations range from .83 (class discussions) and .80 (group projects) down to .40 (lectures/notes/readings), all significant, indicating social presence permeates even nominally 'individual' activities. Open-ended responses converge on interaction/feedback/other-students'-perspectives as the most-cited reason (59%) for an activity's perceived benefit, reinforcing the quantitative pattern.

sections.title: IV. Discussion
sections.summary: Walks each hypothesis: social presence-learning and social presence-satisfaction relations both hold, though instructor satisfaction correlates with perceived learning at least as strongly as social presence does, and the survey's single satisfaction item may have partly absorbed the social-presence construct (a measurement-overlap caveat the authors flag rather than resolve). The predictor finding is triangulated against Gunawardena & Zittle (58% of CMC satisfaction variance from social presence) and Boverie et al. Gender's small effect is left as underdetermined among instrument-bias, sample-specific, and broader-literature explanations. Limitations: self-selected respondent sample, no randomization/control (intact-group design), and an atypical (nontraditional, returning-student) population that limits generalization to traditional undergraduates.

sections.title: V. Conclusions
sections.summary: Argues, from sociocognitive theory (Vygotsky; cooperative-learning literature) plus the study's findings, for a 'better' online-course model that integrates social aspects of learning into design and instruction rather than only delivering content. Calls for further research on the mechanisms of social presence in online environments and on instructor practices that convey it.

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: central construct; averaged Likert composite adapted from Gunawardena & Zittle's scale; treated as a joint property of medium and communicators ('cultured'), not a fixed technological feature

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: operationalized narrowly as self-report *perceived* learning (Likert composite), not measured achievement or retention; predicted by social presence at R2=.46

constructs.label: affect: enjoyment & intrinsic motivation
constructs.treatment: proxied by a single-item instructor-satisfaction measure; authors flag possible measurement overlap with the social-presence construct given item-allocation asymmetry

constructs.label: engagement / flow
constructs.treatment: not separately instrumented; implicated via qualitative finding that interaction/feedback/others'-perspectives is the most-cited (59%) reason activities are perceived as beneficial, read as evidence social presence permeates individual as well as social activities

conditionsNote: Strand F unit, exempt from the media-condition axis per task scope. Design is a single-medium (fully asynchronous, text-based SLN online course), cross-sectional correlational survey with no manipulation, randomization, or control condition ('intact group'); n=97 of 369 enrolled (26% response rate), 63% female, majority age 36-45, nontraditional/returning-student population explicitly flagged by the authors as limiting generalization to traditional undergraduates. No media contrast exists in the design, so no media-condition cell genuinely applies regardless of scope.

readings.claim: Social presence is 'the degree of salience of the other person in the (mediated) interaction and the consequent salience of the interpersonal relationships' — originally a property of the medium (Short, Williams & Christie), later shown to also be a property of communicators' perceptions and behavior ('cultured,' per Gunawardena & Zittle).

Students' overall perceived social presence correlates significantly with overall perceived learning (r=.68) and with instructor satisfaction (r=.60); instructor satisfaction correlates with perceived learning at r=.73, at least as strongly as social presence does.
Students' perceptions of overall social presence are a significant predictor of students' perceived learning (direct-entry regression, R2=.46).

Gender accounts for a small but significant share (R2=.047) of the variability in perceived social presence, with women reporting higher social presence than men; age and college credits earned account for none.

Social presence-perceived learning correlations remain significant across all six course-activity types (.40-.83), including nominally 'individual' activities, indicating social presence permeates the whole course rather than only its overtly collaborative segments.

The single-item instructor-satisfaction measure, set against multiple instructor-interaction-inflected social-presence items, may have partly absorbed the social-presence construct rather than merely correlating with it — an unresolved measurement-overlap caveat.
Sociocognitive theory plus this study's findings jointly argue for a 'better' online-course model integrating social aspects of learning into design and instruction, not only content delivery.

interlocutors.name: Short, John; Williams, Ederyn; Christie, Bruce
interlocutors.role: originators of social-presence theory; source of the medium-salience definition the paper opens with

interlocutors.name: Gunawardena, Charlotte N. & Zittle, Frank J. (1997)
interlocutors.role: direct instrument source (social-presence scale adapted for this study) and direct empirical comparator (58% CMC-satisfaction-variance figure); corresponds to ped-sec-25 in this cluster

interlocutors.name: Wiener, Morton & Mehrabian, Albert
interlocutors.role: originators of the teacher-immediacy construct (psychological distance), treated as a related, possibly subsumed strand

interlocutors.name: Boverie, Patricia; Nagel, Linda; McGee, Michael; Garcia, Sandra
interlocutors.role: comparator study finding social presence the sole significant predictor of distance-education satisfaction among learning-style, emotional-intelligence, and social-presence candidates

interlocutors.name: Moore, A.; Masterson, J.T.; Christophel, D.M.; Shea, K.A.
interlocutors.role: teacher-immediacy literature corroborating immediacy behaviors' link to instruction ratings and satisfaction

interlocutors.name: Vygotsky, Lev
interlocutors.role: sociocognitive-theory source for the 'learning as social/interactive construction' framing used in the conclusion

interlocutors.name: Bullen, Mark
interlocutors.role: case-study source for the face-to-face-lack critique of online learning that the paper's introduction rebuts

tensions.axis: social presence as an inherent property of the medium vs. social presence as culturable by communicators regardless of medium
tensions.note: The paper explicitly sides with Gunawardena & Zittle's culturing revision over Short/Williams/Christie's original medium-determinist framing, treating a purely text-based asynchronous medium as capable of high perceived social presence.

tensions.axis: social presence as a distinct predictor vs. social presence as measurement-confounded with instructor satisfaction
tensions.note: The authors' own regression and correlation results support social presence as a genuine predictor, but they flag that the survey's item-allocation asymmetry (many social-presence items, one satisfaction item) leaves the two constructs' independence unresolved.

tensions.axis: social presence as belonging to overtly 'social' activities vs. social presence permeating nominally 'individual' activities
tensions.note: Significant correlations across all six activity types, including individual projects and self-tests, push against a clean social/individual activity dichotomy.
